problem.text: The least common multiple of a positive integer $n$ and $18$ is $180$, and the greatest common divisor of $n$ and $45$ is $15$. What is the sum of the digits of $n$?

steps.title: Where to start: factor everything into primes
steps.body: LCM and GCD questions are easiest with prime factorizations, because both are decided one prime at a time. Here $18 = 2\cdot 3^2$ and $45 = 3^2\cdot 5$. Since $n$ divides its LCM with $18$, $n$ also divides $180$, so $n$ can only use the primes $2$, $3$ and $5$.

your_turn.prompt: Write $180$ as a product of prime powers.

steps.title: Use the LCM: take the bigger exponent
steps.body: For each prime, the LCM uses the larger of the two exponents. The LCM has $2^2$, but $18$ has only $2^1$, so $n$ must supply the $2^2$. In the same way, $18$ has no $5$, so $n$ must supply the $5$. The power of $3$ in $n$ can be anything up to $2$, because $18$ already has $3^2$.

your_turn.answer: Then neither $n$ nor $18$ has $2^2$, so the LCM would have only $2^1$, not $2^2$.

steps.title: Use the GCD: take the smaller exponent
steps.body: The GCD uses the smaller exponent for each prime. Write the power of $3$ in $n$ as $3^b$. Since $45$ has $3^2$ and $\gcd(n,45) = 15 = 3\cdot 5$, we need $\min(b,2) = 1$.

your_turn.answer: $b=1$. If $b=2$, the GCD would contain $3^2$ and be $45$, not $15$.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: So $n = 2^2\cdot 3\cdot 5 = 60$. Check: $\text{lcm}(60,18) = 180$ and $\gcd(60,45) = 15$. The digit sum is $6+0 = 6$. The answer is **(B)** $6$.

wrong_choices.D: This comes from guessing $n = 180$ from the LCM alone. But $\gcd(180,45) = 45$, not $15$, so the GCD condition rules it out.
wrong_choices.A: This comes from $n = 30$, which forgets that $n$ must supply the $2^2$. Check: $\text{lcm}(30,18) = 90$, not $180$.
